title: Attachment, Love & Relationship Patterns
description: Explore what attachment theory can explain through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: When silence feels like distance
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of what attachment theory can explain.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Attachment processes concern seeking closeness when a relationship feels uncertain. Checking can temporarily reduce uncertainty while leaving the next period of silence to provoke the same fear. The particular relationship and its history matter; one anxious evening cannot reveal an enduring attachment style.

Sometimes delayed replies really do signal unreliable communication. The relevant evidence includes what the couple agreed and how often expectations are unmet.
nodes.sources: Mikulincer & Shaver, Attachment in Adulthood (2016).

nodes.scenario: Nina and Eli have been dating for six months. Eli usually replies during lunch, but today his phone is off while he is travelling.

evidenceOptions.label: Nina may have recently experienced broken promises from Eli, in which case concern about his reliability could reflect current evidence.

responseOptions.label: If you don't reply on time, I'm going to stop messaging you altogether.
I understand you can't always respond. When travel interrupts contact, could we agree when to check in, and also talk about what I tend to assume?

nodes.title: If the first response fails
nodes.prompt: The other person rejects a reasonable direct request and the practical concern is unresolved. What next?
nodes.conceptId: attachment-module-01:Attachment working models and threat appraisal
nodes.explanation: Escalation can be proportionate when a direct attempt has failed. Its safety and usefulness depend on the situation. Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.

options.label: Repeat reassurance until the other person no longer experiences the issue as threatening.
options.feedback: Reassurance can help but cannot guarantee action on a concrete problem.

options.label: If you don't reply on time, I'm going to stop messaging you altogether.
options.feedback: This makes the unresolved issue reviewable without needing to diagnose the other person.

options.label: Drop the matter to avoid further discomfort, regardless of the practical consequences.
options.feedback: Leaving can sometimes be safest, but here it sacrifices the stated practical goal without necessity.

options.label: Can you tell me what you thought the silence meant to me?
options.feedback: A further question can clarify motives, but may delay resolution when the refusal is already clear.

nodes.title: What might change next?
nodes.prompt: The other person may disagree. Which response-and-outcome pairing best protects the practical concern without assuming cooperation?
nodes.conceptId: attachment-module-01:Attachment working models and threat appraisal
nodes.explanation: A sound response is judged by what it makes possible, not by whether it can instantly change somebody else. I understand you can't always respond. When travel interrupts contact, could we agree when to check in, and also talk about what I tend to assume?
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.

outcomes.label: The other person’s interpretation may become clearer, though the original issue may still need to be resolved.
A concrete correction or next step is proposed. Agreement remains uncertain.

nodes.title: Correct the inference
nodes.prompt: Someone says: “That tells us what sort of person they really are.” Which revision is most defensible?
nodes.conceptId: attachment-module-01:Attachment working models and threat appraisal
nodes.explanation: A working interpretation can be informative without being a diagnosis. Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

options.label: Because an alternative is possible, every explanation should be treated as equally likely until we know the person well.
options.feedback: Possible explanations need not be equally supported. We should compare their fit with the actual evidence.

options.label: The behaviour may serve the proposed function in this case. We would need broader evidence before treating it as a stable characteristic.
options.feedback: This retains a useful process explanation without generalising beyond the evidence.

options.label: The person has not confirmed their own motive, so we should avoid making any psychological inference at all.
options.feedback: Direct self-report helps, but a tentative formulation can still be tested against observed circumstances.

options.label: The response fits the theory, so it is likely to occur in most situations that threaten the person.
options.feedback: Generalising to different settings requires repeated observations, not theoretical resemblance alone.

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?
nodes.prompt: You want to distinguish the working hypothesis from its strongest alternative. Which investigation would provide the most discriminating information?
nodes.conceptId: attachment-module-01:Attachment working models and threat appraisal
nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Compare Nina's responses across relationships and circumstances, and examine Eli's actual communication history.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

options.label: Ask both people to describe how strongly they felt during the conversation.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Compare Nina's responses across relationships and circumstances, and examine Eli's actual communication history.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A friend cancels one arrangement because of illness. Another friend interprets the cancellation as a sign that the friendship is fading.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: Apply the method elsewhere
nodes.prompt: Consider this different situation: A friend cancels one arrangement because of illness. Another friend interprets the cancellation as a sign that the friendship is fading. What is the strongest next step?
nodes.conceptId: attachment-module-01:Attachment working models and threat appraisal
nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: Fact or inference?
nodes.prompt: Sort the exact words spoken from explanations about what those words might mean.
nodes.conceptId: attachment-module-01:Attachment working models and threat appraisal
nodes.explanation: The words are evidence. Both the preferred explanation and its rival are interpretations requiring further testing. Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
A temporary absence of contact is being interpreted through an expectation about relational availability. Attachment-related expectations can guide what a person notices and how they respond.

Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
